The Effect of Different Soil Additives and 
Arbuscular Mycorrhizal Fungi on the Growth 
of Bush Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris) and Dry 
Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris) in Mars Regolith 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Plant Mars challenge | Fall 2025 | Middle School Division 
 Stem Sisters Team 
Cassidy M., Annaliese A., Merrill R., Quinn Q. 
 
 
+”_?

Introduction 
Our mission was to help astronauts maximize growth of edible plants on Mars. We 
started by researching the properties of Mars regolith. Compared to Earth soil, Mars 
regolith is very dense in mineral matter, highly toxic, high in pH, and the temperatures 
are extremely cold1. The biggest difference between Earth soil and Mars soil is that 
Mars regolith contains no organic matter, something we know plants need to grow and 
thrive. 
 
We knew that it would be quite hard to grow plants in Mars regolith because of the lack 
of organic material, so we decided to improve the soil with fungi and several different 
soil additives. Arbuscular Mycorrhizal Fungi (AMF) (Rhizophagus Irregularis) is a fungus 
that has been used in agriculture and acts as a root stimulator. This fungus forms a 
beneficial relationship with plants. The fungus captures water and nutrients from the soil 
and transfers to the plant. In exchange, the plant provides food for the fungus. This 
partnership enhances the plant's stress tolerance, improves nutrient and water uptake, 
and can even contribute to better soil structure2. Fruits and vegetables grown for their 
large size, like those that have been noted in The Guinness Book of World Records 
have been rumored to use this fungi in the potting soil3. We live in Colorado which has 
been devastated by forest fires. We know that fire-loving fungi are often the first 
organisms to grow post-fire and fungi can help soil recover from fire by decomposing 
burnt matter4. This is another reason our team wanted to add AMF to the soil to see if it 
would help with Mars regolith recover quickly and allow for plant growth. 
 
Based on our research, we identified a number of soil additives that can boost AMF 
growth in soil. We tested: Biochar, Coffee Grounds, Coconut oil, and Oats. The control 
was simply adding AMF potting soil with Mars regolith and no soil additive. Other 
projects have focused on the use of AMF and Bone Meal, but our team would like to 
see if AMF performed differently with different soil additives.

For seed selection, we picked bean varieties based on the proven relationship between 
beans and AMF. Bush beans were selected because they have a shorter time to 
maturation and would produce vegetables for the astronauts in 60 days. In addition to 
bush beans, we added a dry bean to our design. The superior nutritional value of the 
dry bean to the bush bean would allow astronauts a richer diet in space. See Table 2.

Procedure 
Supplies: 
●​ Mars Regolith 
●​ Protective Gear (masks, gloves) 
●​ Grow Light 
●​ Pots for planting 
●​ Potting soil 
●​ AMF (Trifecta Myco Supreme Plant Root Stimulator for Tree, Rose, and 
Flower Care, Mycorrhizal Fungi) 
●​ PH test strips 
●​ Ruler 
●​ Distilled water 
●​ Bloom City Organic Worm tea Concentrate and compost and Bokashi 
Booster 
●​ Biochar (Plantonix char bliss premium quality BioChar) 
●​ Oats (Coaches Oats Organic Oatmeal - ground into a powder) 
●​ Pine needles (Gathered from the outdoors, ground into a powder) 
●​ Coffee (Brewed Coffee grounds) 
●​ Coconut Oil (365 by Whole Foods Market Organic Refined Coconut oil) 
●​ Bushsnap Beans (Phaseolus vulgaris) 
●​ Dry Bean (Phaseolus vulgaris) 
 
Working outdoors on planting day (Figure 1), the potting soil was mixed with AMF. The 
potting soil/AMF mixture and soil additives were added to pots based on the following 
ratio: Mars Regolith (50%), Potting Soil/AMF (40%), Soil Additive (10%). For the control, 
we added 10% extra plain potting soil in place of Soil Additive. The soil additives that 
were used were Biochar, Pine Needles, Coconut oil, Coffee Grounds, and Oats. There 
were two pots of each additive and bean so for each additive, there were four pots. See 
Figure 2.

Figure 1: Planting Day 
 
 
 
Figure 2: Experimental design demonstrating soil composition and seed selection 
 
Throughout this experiment, the plants were all kept under a constant grow light. The 
plants were watered every other day with a combination of distilled water and worm tea. 
Worm tea was used to add additional organic matter to the growing conditions. Distilled 
water was used because tap water contains chlorine and this could be harmful to AMF. 
 
Our initial planting resulted in only 2 seeds germinating. Most of the soil pots had a solid 
crust which probably inhibited growth as it would be hard for water and oxygen to break 
through this layer. After 14 days, we realized that many of the seeds probably weren’t 
going to germinate so we received authorization to replant. This time, instead of 
germinating the seeds in the soil mixture, we germinated the seeds in a dark 
environment between moist paper towels. When the germinated seeds grew roots and

their first leaves, we transplanted them into the original soil pots. Before the replanting, 
we tilled the soils in the pots hoping to aerate and eliminate that crust that had 
developed. We did not see seeds when we tilled. Based on availability at the local 
hardware store, we used different beans in the replanting. We were still able to replant 
using a dry bean and a bush bean. 
 
Once a week, the pH of the soil was measured. The height (cm) of the plant was also 
measured from the top of the soil to the tallest part of the stretched out plant. Because 
of the replanting, we had six weeks of growth time. The team made observations and 
drawings of the seedling progress. See Figure 3. 
 
 Figure 3: Data Collection (pH, Measurement, Moisture Meter, Watering, Observations)

Figure 5: Average Dry Bean Height (cm) by additive per week 
 
Table 3 shows the average Dry Bean height over 6 weeks. Over those six weeks, all of 
the Dry Beans grew at a pretty steady pace. Some plants grew better than others. 
Seedlings grown with the Coffee additive grew to be the tallest (23.4 cm) and the 
smallest was seedlings grown with the Pine additive (13.75). All of the bean plants on 
average grew at least to be 13 cm tall. 
 
Figure 5 shows a line graph of average Dry bean height over a six week growth period. 
Seedlings grown with Coffee, Biochar, Control (potting soil), and Oats were the better 
performing additives. Unfortunately we didn’t run descriptive statistics on the data so we 
don't know for sure but with the line graph we can infer that they would be the highest 
performing additives.

Figure 6: Average Bush Bean height (cm) by additive per week 
 
Table 4 shows the average Bush Bean height by additive over a six week growing 
period. All seedlings showed growth except for the seedlings grown in Coconut additive 
which died on week 3. The seedlings grown with Oats additive appear to have the 
largest growth (45.3 cm) while the seedlings grown in Coconut additive appear to have 
the smallest growth (0 cm) followed by the Pine (16.15cm) and Biochar (16.15cm). 
 
Figure 6 shows the Average Bush Bean height over a six week growing period. 
Seedlings grown in Oats and Control (potting soil) additives appear to have the best 
growth, although because statistics weren’t used to analyze the data, it isn’t possible to 
back up that assumption with specific p-value.

pages.text:
Conclusion 
Our main goal in this experiment was to help astronauts maximize growth of edible 
plants on Mars. While we expected there to be a major difference in seedling growth 
between the soil additives, the addition of any organic matter and AMF to Mars regolith 
appeared to aid in plant growth. Overall, we found that all the plants grew equally 
around the same height except for coconut. Because many forms of organic matter aid 
in plant growth, finding a source of organic matter that doesn’t need to be transported to 
Mars would be the most effective. If astronauts converted their bodily and other waste 
into Biochar on Mars, and used this Biochar in addition to AMF it would be the best 
possible solution to make healthy, food producing plants. 
 
Measuring the seedlings was a bit of a challenge as this differed from person to person 
even though we tried to standardize the process. This might account for some of the 
height measurements from week to week decreasing when in fact most plants grew 
over that same time. In future experiments, we might assign one person to make all of 
the height measurements to be more consistent. We also could standardize watering. At 
first, we may have over-watered plants as the run-off produced a rotten, stinky 
environment. Eventually, we settled on a smaller amount of water (just enough to 
saturate but not run out of the pot) and a more frequent watering schedule. 
 
Seedlings in the Coconut additive were particularly hard to grow. Two of the second 
plantings died fairly soon after replanting and subsequently three died out of four. We 
think the oily conditions were not suitable for plant growth. 
 
Sample size of the experiment made running statistics on data challenging. When even 
one plant died (Biochar) it was hard to make assumptions but when three died for 
Coconut we basically had to end the trial. 
 
If we were to do this experiment again, we would grow 20 biochar plants to find a 
trendline or run statistics to see if there was a difference between a soil additive like 
Biochar and regular potting soil. We would also select plant pots that were all the same 
color so that if the light reflected off of them the plants would be under the same light 
conditions. If we were to do this experiment again we would use coconut oil spray 
instead of the solid oil so it would only coat a little bit of the soil instead of causing the 
soil to be too greasy. We would also control the amount of water we are giving the 
plants so that they are all getting an equal share of the water. We could have used all 
the same color of popsicle sticks or undyed popsicle sticks so that the dye wouldn't 
affect the growth of the plant.
